title: Geroscience & Regenerative Biology
description: Mechanisms linking aging biology to tissue resilience, damage response, senescence, stem-cell function, and regeneration—taught with evidence appraisal and translational caution.

modifications: 2026-10-07: added four original lessons (survival and healthspan endpoints; senescent-cell causality; clonal hematopoiesis and circulating factors; aging clocks and partial reprogramming) beside the preserved legacy units; retagged the four legacy checks to the objectives they assess.

prerequisites.statement: Cell biology; Genetics; Biochemistry; Biostatistics recommended

outcomes.description: Distinguish organismal aging mechanisms from correlates.
Interpret senescence and stem-cell assays with controls.
Evaluate causal evidence for an intervention.
Separate lifespan, healthspan, and tissue-function endpoints.

lesson_objectives.description: Compare damage, maintenance, and adaptation models.
Distinguish biomarker change from improved function.
Define senescence operationally using multiple features.
Distinguish cell-state evidence from a single marker.
Relate stem-cell function to niche signals and tissue demand.
Distinguish cell number from self-renewal and differentiation capacity.
Evaluate whether an intervention's mechanism is supported by its endpoints.
Design a study that separates efficacy from toxicity or selection effects.
Calculate an interval death probability and a Gompertz mortality-rate doubling time from cohort data.
Distinguish lifespan, healthspan, and tissue-function endpoints, including the effects of censoring and survivor selection.
Evaluate whether a lifespan study's design supports the generality of its claim.
Compare genetic and pharmacologic senescent-cell clearance designs and state what each can establish.
Calculate intention-to-treat and survivor-only response estimates and explain how treatment-related dropout biases efficacy.
Identify mechanism-linked senolytic toxicities and select measurements that would detect them.
Explain clonal expansion in an aging stem-cell pool and convert a variant allele fraction into an estimated clone size.
Evaluate heterochronic parabiosis and blood-exchange designs, separating dilution of old-blood factors from supply of young-blood factors.
Identify assay-specificity and replication problems in claims about single circulating factors.
Explain how epigenetic clocks are trained and calculate age acceleration as a residual from a reference calibration.
Evaluate whether a clock change supports rejuvenation, considering noise, cell composition, regression to the mean, and identity loss.
Design measurements for a partial-reprogramming experiment that separate youthful features from dedifferentiation and tumor risk.
Estimate a mutation-accumulation rate from cross-sectional counts and state the assumptions that make a rate meaningful.
Use the damage-maintenance balance to explain why equal burden can arise from different causes and name measurements that separate them.
Evaluate what a repair-deficiency syndrome does and does not show about normal aging.
Calculate autophagic flux from marker levels measured with and without a lysosomal inhibitor and interpret the result.
Distinguish induction of a quality-control pathway from blocked degradation when a marker rises.
Evaluate evidence that proteostasis or mitochondrial changes are causes rather than consequences of aging in a tissue.
Calculate percent change in median and in late-life survival and explain why they answer different questions.
Explain how insulin/IGF, TOR and AMPK signaling link nutrient state to growth and maintenance programs.
Evaluate conflicting results from two studies of the same intervention by comparing their designs.
Calculate and compare scar fraction between injury conditions from replicate measurements.
Distinguish proliferation markers, hypertrophy and true regeneration, and name the evidence needed to claim regeneration.
Explain what comparisons across species and across developmental time can and cannot say about adult mammals.
Compute a per-group sample size for a two-group comparison from a standardized effect size and state its assumptions.
Evaluate a summary of a lifespan or healthspan study for multiplicity, sex and strain, blinding and endpoint choice.
Distinguish statistical significance, effect size and importance when reporting an intervention effect.
Convert event rates to absolute and relative risk reduction and the number needed to treat and interpret each.
Place a claim on an evidence ladder from cell culture to randomized human trial and name what is missing at each step.
Evaluate whether a biomarker change is an acceptable surrogate for a clinical outcome.
Calculate the intraclass correlation coefficient from between-person and within-person variance and interpret it as test–retest reliability.
Compute the smallest detectable change for an individual and show how averaging repeated measurements improves it.
Evaluate whether a biomarker can serve as a surrogate endpoint for an intervention, distinguishing prediction from causal mediation.
Specify a primary endpoint, comparison and analysis for an aging-intervention study in advance, and justify the choice between lifespan and healthspan endpoints.
Estimate the number of deaths and animals needed to detect a stated hazard ratio with a survival comparison.
Evaluate a study design for the safeguards that prevent false positives: randomization, blinding, both sexes, multiple sites, pre-registration and handling of censoring and survivor bias.
Summarize a lifespan cohort correctly when some animals are still alive at the end of the study, using counts and Kaplan–Meier medians rather than naive means.
Identify survivorship bias in a healthspan measure taken only in animals alive at a late time point.
Evaluate which conclusions a single synthetic cohort supports about an intervention's effect on lifespan and healthspan.

duration.equivalent_structure: Proposed 14-week undergraduate scope only. Weeks 1 to 12 pair the compact prototype units with original lessons on mechanisms, measurement, regeneration and evidence appraisal; week 13 is a synthetic-data lifespan lab and week 14 a study-design lesson with the course case. All activities are open, ungraded practice. There are no graded homework sets, exams or project, and workload has not been measured, so this schedule is not evidence of semester equivalence.

lessons.title: Aging as a systems process
lessons.worked_example: A change in an epigenetic clock after intervention does not by itself show that tissue function or healthspan improved; both should be measured independently.

lessons.title: Survival curves, mortality hazards, and healthspan endpoints
lessons.worked_example: If monthly hazard rises from 0.010 at 18 months to 0.040 at 30 months, G = ln 4/12 ≈ 0.116 per month and the mortality-rate doubling time is about 6.0 months. A group with half the hazard at every age keeps the same doubling time yet lives longer, so doubling time and median lifespan answer different questions.

lessons.title: Senescence, inflammation, and tissue context
lessons.worked_example: A senescence-associated β-galactosidase-positive cell is not conclusive alone; a panel plus evidence of persistent arrest and appropriate controls is stronger.

lessons.title: Clearance models, senolytics, and dropout-aware efficacy
lessons.worked_example: With 40 animals per arm, 19 of 38 vehicle survivors and 20 of 32 senolytic survivors improved, an apparent 12.5-point benefit. Counting the deaths as not improved gives 47.5% versus 50.0%, a 2.5-point difference: treatment-related deaths removed animals unlikely to improve, so survivors alone overstate benefit.

modules.title: Stem cells, niches, and regenerative capacity

lessons.title: Stem cells, niches, and regenerative capacity
lessons.worked_example: An expanded progenitor population after injury may reflect compensatory proliferation; it does not establish durable self-renewal or restoration of organ function.

modules.title: Aging stem-cell pools and circulating factors

lessons.title: Clonal hematopoiesis and circulating-factor claims
lessons.worked_example: If 72 of 800 reads carry a DNMT3A variant, the variant allele fraction is 0.09. For a heterozygous autosomal mutation without copy-number change, about 2 × 0.09 = 18% of sampled nucleated cells carry it; a binomial standard error near 0.010 already makes 0.07–0.11 plausible.

lessons.title: Intervention evidence and translational design
lessons.worked_example: If a senolytic improves function only in animals that tolerate a high dose, reporting survivors alone can exaggerate benefit; intent-to-treat and toxicity analyses are essential.

lessons.title: Aging clocks and partial-reprogramming rejuvenation claims
lessons.worked_example: With a calibration clock age = 4 + 0.92 × chronological age, a 50-year-old reading 55 has age acceleration 55 − 50 = +5 years, while an 80-year-old reading 80 has +2.4 years despite a raw difference of zero. Selecting people for high acceleration guarantees some decline on retest, so a randomized control is required.

lessons.title: Genome instability and repair capacity: damage, maintenance and what accumulates
lessons.worked_example: Tissue A rises from 410 to 1990 substitutions per cell over 60 years, an average of 26.33 per year, about 4.9 times Tissue B; old cultures remove a mean fraction 0.545 against 0.7175 for young, a ratio of 0.76.

lessons.title: Proteostasis, autophagy and mitochondria: quality control and what changes with age
lessons.worked_example: Young flux is 3.0 − 1.0 = 2.0 and old flux is 2.4 − 1.8 = 0.6, a ratio of 0.30, even though old cells have the higher resting LC3-II; 34 of 200 cells (17%) exceed a 70% heteroplasmy threshold.

lessons.title: Nutrient sensing and lifespan interventions: what the model organisms show
lessons.worked_example: Median survival rises from 800 to 880 days, a 10.0% change, while the longest-lived-decile mean rises from 1000 to 1060, a 6.0% change; with 60 animals per group the decile rests on 6 animals.

lessons.title: Regeneration across species: what regrows, what scars, and what counts as evidence
lessons.worked_example: Mean scar area is 3.2% after day-1 resection and 18.4% after day-7 resection, 15.2 percentage points apart against a sham mean of 0.5%; higher EdU labeling (5.2% against 0.8%) fits renewed cell-cycle activity but does not show new cardiomyocytes.

lessons.title: Reading an aging-intervention paper: design, power and what a result is worth
lessons.worked_example: For d = 0.5 at α = 0.05 and 80% power, n = 2 × (1.96 + 0.84)² / 0.25 = 62.72, so 63 per group; twelve independent endpoints at α = 0.05 give a 0.460 chance of at least one false positive with no true effects.

lessons.title: From model to human: evidence tiers, surrogate markers and honest limits
lessons.worked_example: Event rates of 10% and 8% give ARR 0.02, RRR 20% and NNT 50; a lower biomarker score supports a statement about the score, not about aging, unless it is shown to be a surrogate for the outcome.

lessons.title: Biomarkers of aging under scrutiny: reliability, the smallest detectable change and surrogate endpoints
lessons.worked_example: With between-person SD 5 and within-person SD 3 years, ICC = 0.735 and the smallest detectable individual change is 8.3 years, falling to 4.8 years when 3 measurements are averaged; a 4-year drop from two single readings is within noise.

lessons.title: Designing a credible aging-intervention study: endpoints, power for survival, and safeguards against fooling ourselves
lessons.worked_example: Detecting a hazard ratio of 0.8 with 80% power at α = 0.05 needs about 631 deaths, roughly 788 animals if 80% die; HR 0.7 needs 247; 400 animals with 320 deaths can detect only about a 27% reduction in death rate.

modules.title: Virtual laboratory: lifespan cohort with censoring and survivor bias

lessons.title: Virtual lab 1: a lifespan cohort with censoring and a survivor-only healthspan test
lessons.worked_example: The Kaplan–Meier median is day 760 in the control group and day 821 in the intervention group, where two animals are censored at day 1000; treating them as deaths gives a biased mean of 836.5 days. Grip strength at day 730 exists for 8 control and 10 intervention survivors, so the means of 90.5 and 92.5 g compare different survivor subsets.

grading_policy.attempt_policy: Unlimited formative retries; no summative grade is awarded.
grading_policy.solution_release: Public practice solutions may be shown after an attempt. They are not production exam keys.
grading_policy.late_policy: No deadlines or late penalties exist in this partial package.
grading_policy.appeals: No instructor review workflow is implemented; report ambiguous practice items to repository maintainers.

accessibility.diagram_policy: The seed package contains no imported diagrams; newly authored diagrams require descriptions and individual license tracking.
known_issues: Unicode equations require structured mathematical alternatives and assistive-technology review.

history.summary: Preserved original compact prototype content in separate manifests and readings; labeled partial without semester or credit equivalency.

Added four original lessons with explicitly synthetic data tables, worked examples, 15 formative items, 16 retrieval cards, and 21 link-only scientific references: survival curves, Gompertz hazards and healthspan endpoints; genetic and pharmacologic senescent-cell clearance with dropout-aware efficacy; clonal hematopoiesis and circulating-factor claims; and epigenetic clocks with partial reprogramming. Mapped every lesson objective to a course outcome and retagged the four legacy checks to the objectives they assess. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Added six original lessons with explicitly synthetic data tables, worked examples, 30 formative items with computed keys, 24 retrieval cards and link-only references verified on 2026-10-08: genome instability and repair capacity; proteostasis, autophagy and mitochondria (flux versus level); nutrient sensing and lifespan interventions (including conflicting primate studies); regeneration across species and what counts as evidence; reading an aging-intervention paper (sample size, multiplicity); and evidence tiers from model to human (absolute and relative effects, surrogates). The lessons make no claim that any intervention slows or reverses human aging. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Added an original lesson on biomarker reliability (ICC, smallest detectable change) and surrogate endpoints, with no claim that any intervention changes human aging with synthetic data, formative items with computed keys and retrieval cards. The package remains partial and unreviewed.

Added a proposed 14-week schedule, a synthetic lifespan-cohort virtual lab (censoring, Kaplan–Meier medians and survivor bias in a late healthspan measure) and an original study-design lesson (endpoints, deaths needed for a survival comparison, safeguards against false positives). All activities remain ungraded practice; the package remains partial and unreviewed and makes no claim about human aging.

Assessments with items now also list the course outcomes those items assess, derived from each item's lesson objective and that objective's outcome links. The rubric-only case lists none. No readings, items or keys changed. The syllabus version line was updated. The course limitations shown to learners were also updated: they still described the package before its 14-week schedule, lab and new lessons, and said some objectives had no practice item. The package remains partial, unreviewed and formative-only.

limitations: Four compact legacy units are preserved beside 13 original readings, including one synthetic-data virtual lab; this package is not equivalent to a full university semester.

A proposed 14-week schedule exists but is unmeasured and unreviewed. There is one synthetic-data virtual lab and no substantive homework sequence, laboratory sequence, midterm, cumulative final, or graded integrative project.

Practice items are short formative checks (two per prototype unit and three to six per original lesson); they do not demonstrate comprehensive outcome coverage or mastery, and objective associations remain provisional.
Bloom labels, objective-to-outcome links, and structured prerequisite edges are authoring classifications awaiting subject-matter review.
All data tables in the new lessons are synthetic teaching data; cited studies are summarized qualitatively from link-only references and are not reproduced.
Question answers and solution feedback are intentionally public practice authoring specifications, not restricted exam keys.

Of the 31 numerical answers in this package, one requires a unit, five check significant figures and none checks dimensions; the others accept a number within a stated tolerance, with the unit optional.
Total workload and weekly duration are unknown; former nominal credit values and hardcoded reading times do not establish workload.
intentionally_omitted: Graded assessments and a laboratory sequence are not authored yet (one synthetic-data virtual lab exists); the original lessons extend a partial package.
No dosing, treatment, supplement, or clinical-test recommendations are given; intervention content is limited to evidence appraisal.
